subject: modeling the difference between two Binomials?

messages.author: 38a3aacdb5d6f07c
messages.subject: modeling the difference between two Binomials?
parts:
Hi INLA community, 

I'm new to INLA, coming from Stan. In Stan we have a model:

Y_i^treatment ~ Binomial(N_i^treatment, p_i^treatment)
Y_i^control ~ Binomial(N_i^control, p_i^control)

p_i^treatment - p_i^control ~ Normal(X_i * beta, sigma)

where X_i * beta is a multilevel model.

But our Stan model fits too slowly for our purposes. 

Is this likelihood possible to implement in INLA?

Thanks so much!
Shira

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] modeling the difference between two Binomials?
parts:
Hi,

Are you sure this is what you want? A Gaussian distribution can be larger than 1, but the difference between two probabilities cannot.

PS: For us, it is easier to answer the question if you write it fully out as a GAM/GLMM.

Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] modeling the difference between two Binomials?
parts:
I agree with Haakon.

I would guess what you mean is that you have a joint model, one for
treatment and one for control

so

y^t ~ treatment
y^c ~ control

and then you want to impose a model for the difference as well

y^t ~ treatment - 1/2 * difference
y^c ~ control + 1/2 * difference

where the 'difference' is the difference model

this is on the logit/probit scale.

messages.author: 38a3aacdb5d6f07c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] modeling the difference between two Binomials?
parts:
Thanks so much!

We are doing a meta-analysis with interest in heterogeneity of effects by randomized experiment j and population subgroup g (a cross-classification of 3 factors: g1, g2, g3). Outcomes are binary.

Let Y_jgt = number of successes in experiment j, subgroup g, treatment group t, out of a sample size of n_jgt.

Y_jgt ~ Binomial(n_jgt, p_jgt)

logit(p_jgt) ~ Normal(a_0 + a_g1 + a_g2 + a_g3 + a_j + b_0*t + b_g1 * t + b_g2 * t + b_g3 * t + b_j * t, sigma)

priors:
a_g1 ~ Normal(0, sigma_1)
a_g2 ~ Normal(0, sigma_2)
a_g3 ~ Normal(0, sigma_3)
a_j ~ Normal(0, sigma_experiment)
b_g1 ~ Normal(0, sigma_1_interaction)
b_g2 ~ Normal(0, sigma_2_interaction)
b_g3 ~ Normal(0, sigma_3_interaction)
b_j ~ Normal(0, sigma_experiment_interaction)

Our Stan model then has a hyperprior that jointly estimates the scales:
sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3, sigma_experiment ~ Normal^+(0, sigma_main)
sigma_1_interaction, sigma_2_interaction, sigma_3_interaction, sigma_experiment_interaction ~ Normal^+(0, sigma_interaction)

We have weakly-informative priors on the remaining parameters.

Is the above model possible to fit in INLA? (Modifications welcome!)

Our modeling task is similar to p.239-244 of Bayesian Data Analysis 3rd edition (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/book/). Their model does not logit-transform, though we can as you recommend! In my original conception, we were modeling the treatment effects p_jg1 - p_jg0 directly, which in our particular application area are far enough from -1 and 1 for a Normal to have been acceptable.

Thanks again!!
Shira

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] modeling the difference between two Binomials?
parts:
Thanks so much!

Something like the below? 

"data_point" is the row of the dataset dat, where each row gives successes y out of trials n. The random effect for data_point gives what I call "sigma" in my model above, which expresses lack of fit of the linear model (as on p.241 of Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition).

For the PC priors, I tried following p.107-108 of https://www.crcpress.com/Bayesian-Regression-Modeling-with-INLA/Wang-Ryan-Faraway/p/book/9781498727259

y_like <- logit(dat$y/dat$n)
sdres <- sd(y_like[is.finite(y_like)])
pcprior <- list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param = c(3*sdres, 0.01)))

fit_inla = inla(y ~ 1 + f(g1, model="iid", pcprior) + f(g2, model="iid", pcprior) + f(g3, model="iid", pcprior) + f(experiment, model="iid", pcprior) + t + f(data_point, model="iid", pcprior), 
              family="binomial", 
              Ntrials=n, data=dat)

There is no way in INLA to jointly model the sigmas for the random effects, like I had in Stan?

Thanks again,
Shira
